paras: The lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott was the reported hanging of two men accused of horse theft by cowmen in Routt county, Colorado, near the Utah line, in mid-September 1888. The news reached Aspen, where Gillam had lived, as rumor, but papers in Colorado and Montana repeated it as fact.
On the night Gillam left Aspen, K. R. Bowles and a Mr. Plumb each missed a horse, and the two men were said to be driving a band of eighteen horses, part of them from Piceance creek.

Cowmen of the Piceance creek section reportedly pursued the men to the Utah line, captured them and hanged both from a tree, burying them near the spot. A wife of one of the men, with a baby about a month old, was said to have fought to save her husband and, by one account, was threatened with the rope herself.
Plumb sent a man to Routt county to look for his horse among the captured herd; no report of arrests or an inquest appears in the coverage.

The Bent County Register gave the first notice on September 22 in one line: "two horse thieves were caught and lynched in Routt county," without names. The fullest account, from the Aspen Times, reprinted by the Delta Independent on September 25, ran as "A Reported Lynching" and rested on a letter said to be from Mrs. Gillam and the word of a White river cattleman. It noted the story's "wild sensational features" yet described the cowmen choosing "the handiest pine tree that had a limb strong enough to serve as a gallows."

By October 13 the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner, quoting the Ogden Argus under "Hanged by Cowmen," stated the hanging as fact, calling the men "alleged" thieves and the cowmen "self-constituted executioners." No paper gave the race of either man.

The Aspen Times named the woman Mrs. Gillam and put the hanging on a pine, while the Ogden Argus called her Mrs. Elliott and the tree a fir; the Aspen paper, in Gillam's own town, said the news came through her letter.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott
bases: Cowmen are reported to have pursued, captured and hanged two men accused of stealing horses, without any legal process (A2, A3).

All three reports say the two men were hanged, by 'cowmen' whom the Ogden Argus called 'self-constituted executioners', for alleged horse theft (A1, A2, A3); no paper gives the number of cowmen, and the fullest account presents the story as unconfirmed rumor (A2).

Three papers in Colorado and Montana (the last quoting a Utah paper) agree that two horse thieves were caught and lynched in Routt county, and none denies it, though the Aspen Times account is explicitly rumor and the Ogden Argus version may draw on the same sources (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Aspen Times (rumor from a letter and a White river cattleman)
accounts.gist: Rumors from two apparently separate sources said cowmen pursued Gillam and Elliott to the Utah line with eighteen horses, hanged them from a pine and buried them near the spot; Mrs. Gillam fought to save her husband and was threatened with the rope.

accounts.label: Bent County Register brief
accounts.gist: Two unnamed horse thieves were caught and lynched in Routt county early in the week.

accounts.label: Ogden Argus (via Butte Semi-Weekly Miner)
accounts.gist: Piceance creek cowmen overtook Gillam and Elliott near the Utah line and hanged both from a fir branch while Mrs. Elliott, with a month-old baby, fought to protect her husband.

framing.detail: The Aspen Times, under 'A Reported Lynching', presented the story as rumor and remarked on its 'wild sensational features', while describing the hanging tree with some flippancy.
The Bent County Register gave a one-line notice of 'two horse thieves' lynched, without names or comment.
The Ogden Argus account, headed 'Hanged by Cowmen' in Butte, called the men only 'alleged' thieves and the cowmen 'self-constituted executioners', and dwelt on the wife's resistance.

conflicts.note: Both describe a wife with a month-old baby who fought for her husband; the Aspen paper, where Gillam had lived, is likelier to have the name right, but neither is confirmed.

versions.value: the branch of a fir tree

conflicts.note: No local Routt county report or later confirmation appears in the coverage.

record_check.dossier: About September 16-20, 1888 ('fore part of this week' on September 22; 'about five days ago' in the Aspen Times item); no exact date is given.
Unofficial pursuers: 'the cowmen' of Piceance creek; no sheriff or deputized posse is mentioned.
Correct for the Aspen Times, but the Bent County Register and the Ogden Argus (via Butte) stated the lynching as fact; the Argus names the woman present Mrs. Elliott.
3 white papers, 1888-09-22 to 1888-10-13, including the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner quoting the Ogden Argus.
No paper gives the race of either man.
